deck_name: Tarot de Marseille — Nicolas Conver 1760 (The Printed Standard)

major-00-le-mat.name: 0 — The Fool
major-00-le-mat.Scene: Le Mat (The Fool) in the Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille shows a wandering figure in a motley costume — a parti-colored garment of patchwork suggesting the jester or vagrant — walking toward the right edge of the card, his bindle stick over his shoulder. A small dog or animal nips at his leg or backside, tearing at his garment. The Mat is unnumbered (though later prints sometimes number him 0) and is traditionally placed either before or after the trump sequence. Conver's Mat shows the characteristic blue-and-yellow Marseille colorwork, the figure's torn stocking revealing a wound or bare leg, the animal's aggression indifferent to the Mat's cheerful or oblivious stride.

major-01-le-bateleur.name: 1 — The Magician
major-01-le-bateleur.Scene: Le Bateleur (The Juggler/Magician) stands at a table set with his implements — cups, balls, a knife, and other small tools of the street conjurer's trade. His wide-brimmed hat curves up at the sides (or has the lemniscate-like shape that appears in some versions), his coat and breeches in Marseille colors. With his right hand he holds or gestures with a wand, while the left indicates the table. The Bateleur is the showman and sleight-of-hand artist, a figure from popular street performance rather than the learned magician of later occult tarot. In the Conver 1760 woodblock printing, the details of his table and implements are rendered with the characteristic bold lines and primary colors of the Marseille engraving tradition.

major-02-la-papesse.name: 2 — The High Priestess
major-02-la-papesse.Scene: La Papesse (The Popess) is a seated female figure wearing the papal tiara and holding an open book on her lap. She is dressed in the blue and white robes of a female pope — a figure whose iconographic origins have been debated (Pope Joan legend, the Guglielmites, the Visconti allusion to a female figurehead). In the Conver 1760, she is a serene authority figure behind a veil or curtain, the open book on her lap suggesting secret or sacred knowledge withheld from view. The tiara and robes make her an exact feminine counterpart of Le Pape (V), holding spiritual authority in its feminine form.

major-03-limperatrice.name: 3 — The Empress
major-03-limperatrice.Scene: L'Impératrice (The Empress) is a seated female figure bearing the orb and scepter of imperial sovereignty, or sometimes a shield with an eagle. She is crowned with the imperial crown, her posture one of relaxed authority. In the Conver 1760, the Empress is a robust figure of earthly female power — less ethereal than the Popess, more actively governing. Her right hand may hold a scepter while her left bears the orb, or she holds a shield. The characteristic Marseille color palette renders her robes in bold reds, yellows, and blues.

major-04-lempereur.name: 4 — The Emperor
major-04-lempereur.Scene: L'Empereur (The Emperor) is a crowned male figure seated on a throne, his body often turned three-quarters or in profile to show his eagle-emblazoned armor or robes. He holds the scepter of temporal authority, and his posture is one of settled, secure power. In the Conver 1760, the Emperor is rendered in the woodblock style with his crown and imperial regalia, the characteristic Marseille coloring giving his armor and throne the colors of earthly dominion. The throne may show decorative elements or animal heads.

major-05-le-pape.name: 5 — The Hierophant
major-05-le-pape.Scene: Le Pape (The Pope) is an enthroned figure in papal vestments — the triple tiara, the red and white robes of the papacy — with his right hand raised in the blessing gesture and his left holding a triple cross or scepter. Before him kneel two smaller figures (clergy or petitioners), receiving his blessing or instruction. The Pape is the spiritual authority in its male hierarchical form, the institutional head of the sacred order. In the Conver 1760, his tiara and vestments are rendered in the primary colors of the Marseille tradition.

major-06-lamoureux.name: 6 — The Lovers
major-06-lamoureux.Scene: L'Amoureux (The Lovers) in the Conver 1760 shows three figures: a young man at the center stands between two women (one on each side), while above him a winged Cupid draws his bow. This is the traditional Marseille Amoureux — not yet the paired lovers of the Waite-Smith but the scene of a young man's choice between two women, the arrow of love about to strike. The three figures are rendered in the bright woodblock colors of the Marseille tradition, the young man's posture suggesting hesitation or attraction toward one or the other.

major-07-le-chariot.name: 7 — The Chariot
major-07-le-chariot.Scene: Le Chariot (The Chariot) shows a crowned figure standing or seated in a stone canopied vehicle, holding a scepter and wearing armor with epaulettes of two contrasting colors (one blue, one red — representing the opposing forces held in tension). The chariot is drawn by two horses or sphinxes of contrasting colors (one light, one dark). The charioteer does not hold reins but controls the animals through will. In the Conver 1760, the chariot is a massive architectural vehicle with a starry canopy, the contrasting sphinxes or horses below embodying the mastery of opposing forces.

major-08-la-justice.name: 8 — Justice
major-08-la-justice.Scene: La Justice (Justice) is a seated female figure holding the upright sword in her right hand and the scales in her left — the classical allegorical Justice of the Western legal tradition. In the Conver 1760, Justice is rendered frontally, her throne flanked by decorative columns or curtains, her posture upright and her gaze direct. The Conver places Justice at VIII (before Strength at XI), following the Marseille sequence rather than the Waite-Smith transposition.

major-09-lhermite.name: 9 — The Hermit
major-09-lhermite.Scene: L'Hermite (The Hermit) is a solitary old man in a cloak, walking with a staff. He holds a lantern (often six-pointed in the Marseille tradition, rendered as a star-shaped form) in his right hand, raised to illuminate the darkness. His long beard and stooped posture suggest age and spiritual withdrawal. In the Conver 1760, the Hermit faces slightly to the left (toward the past or inward), the lantern held out as the light of inner wisdom carried through the dark. He is the figure of contemplative withdrawal from the social world.

major-10-la-roue.name: 10 — Wheel of Fortune
major-10-la-roue.Scene: La Roue de Fortune (The Wheel of Fortune) shows a large wheel with figures ascending and descending — the conventional iconography of Fortune's turning derived from the Boethian tradition. In the Conver 1760, the wheel shows a crowned figure at the top (Fortune at her peak), figures ascending on one side, and a falling figure on the other. Two animals (often a jackal-headed figure and a snake or rabbit) flank or ride the wheel, and the wheel structure itself is a prominent mechanical element. The Sphinx or crowned figure at the top presides over the rotation.

major-11-la-force.name: 11 — Strength
major-11-la-force.Scene: La Force (Strength/Fortitude) shows a female figure in a broad-brimmed hat, opening or closing the mouth of a lion with her bare hands. The lion stands or kneels before her, and the woman's posture is calm and confident — the virtue of fortitude as the patient mastery of the animal nature rather than violent conquest. In the Conver 1760, the Force card shows the characteristic Marseille hat (a wide, decorated brim with a figure-eight or lemniscate curve) and the woman's gentle-but-firm hold on the lion's jaws. The figure's expression is serene, suggesting moral strength over brute force.

major-12-le-pendu.name: 12 — The Hanged Man
major-12-le-pendu.Scene: Le Pendu (The Hanged Man) shows a figure suspended by one foot from a wooden gallows — a T-shaped or post-and-beam structure with his hands bound behind his back. The Hanged Man's expression in the Conver 1760 is calm or even serene, suggesting willing suspension rather than punishment. His free leg is bent at the knee in the characteristic crossed-legs posture. Two cut branches on the post suggest the living tree converted to instrument of suspension. The figure wears the colored hose and doublet of the Marseille tradition, rendered in the primary woodblock colors.

major-13-la-mort.name: 13 — Death
major-13-la-mort.Scene: La Mort (Death) — the only Marseille trump that appears without a title in the Conver 1760 (the space for the name is blank) — shows a skeletal figure wielding a large scythe that cuts through a field of body parts: severed heads, hands, and feet emerging from the ground. The skeleton walks or strides through the scene, the scythe swinging low. The severed body parts include a crowned head (suggesting no one is exempt from Death's harvest) and a female head. The absence of the name 'La Mort' on the card was a common Marseille convention, the superstition being that naming Death would invoke it.

major-14-temperance.name: 14 — Temperance
major-14-temperance.Scene: Tempérance (Temperance) shows a winged female figure pouring liquid between two vessels — a large ewer and a cup, the liquid flowing in a thin stream. In the Conver 1760, the figure is a standing angel with large blue and red wings, her robes in the Marseille primary colors, the two vessels at different heights allowing the measured transfer of liquid. The pouring is precise and controlled, the virtue of Temperance expressed as the careful management of flow between two containers.

major-15-le-diable.name: 15 — The Devil
major-15-le-diable.Scene: Le Diable (The Devil) in the Conver 1760 shows a large bat-winged figure on a pedestal or platform, with horns, an animal face, and a torch or flaming club. Below him, two smaller chained figures (a male and a female demon or human) stand bound to the pedestal. The Devil figure has clawed feet, animal legs, a secondary face on his belly, and holds his flaming club aloft. The composition follows the conventional Marseille Devil type: the central figure of infernal authority above the two bound lesser figures, the whole scene rendered in the bold woodblock style.

major-16-la-maison-dieu.name: 16 — The Tower
major-16-la-maison-dieu.Scene: La Maison-Dieu (The House of God / The Tower) in the Conver 1760 shows a tall tower being struck by lightning (a bolt or crown-shaped flash from above), with two figures falling head-first from the battlements. The tower structure is typically rendered with a crown at the top that is struck off by the lightning bolt — the crown being separated from the tower by the force of the strike. Flames or sparks emerge from the windows and top of the tower. The two falling figures, in different-colored clothing, arc away from the tower in symmetrical or asymmetric falls.

major-17-letoile.name: 17 — The Star
major-17-letoile.Scene: L'Étoile (The Star) in the Conver 1760 shows a nude female figure kneeling at the edge of a pool or stream, pouring water from two vessels — one onto the water and one onto the land. Above her a large central star (eight-pointed) is surrounded by seven smaller stars in the night sky. Behind her, a bird (often an ibis) perches in a tree. The woman's posture is one of graceful offering, her body unclothed as a sign of natural or divine revelation. The characteristic Marseille Star uses the eight-pointed large star and seven smaller stars above the pouring figure.

major-18-la-lune.name: 18 — The Moon
major-18-la-lune.Scene: La Lune (The Moon) in the Conver 1760 shows a large moon face in the sky (often showing a profile or full face in the disc, surrounded by drops or rays falling toward the earth), while below a pool or stream between two towers is flanked by a lobster or crayfish crawling toward the surface. Two dogs (or a dog and a wolf) bay at the moon from either side. The falling drops or rays create a distinctive shower from the moon to the earth. The scene is night, the dogs on a path between the two towers that frame the distant landscape.

major-19-le-soleil.name: 19 — The Sun
major-19-le-soleil.Scene: Le Soleil (The Sun) in the Conver 1760 shows a large sun face radiating straight and wavy alternating rays toward the earth. Below, two nude children (a boy and a girl, or two boys) stand on earth or play together in front of a low stone wall, their hands perhaps joined. Falling drops or swirling forms descend from the sun. The children's nakedness represents innocence and the joyful return to natural simplicity after the trials of the nocturnal cards. The Conver Sun uses the characteristic alternating straight-and-wavy ray pattern around the solar face.

major-20-le-jugement.name: 20 — Judgement
major-20-le-jugement.Scene: Le Jugement (Judgement) in the Conver 1760 shows a large angel with trumpet descending from above, the blast of the horn summoning three figures — a man, a woman, and a child — who rise from a coffin or from the earth below, their arms raised. The angel above is often shown with a sun-disc behind its head and a blue background. The three rising figures form a family unit: the resurrected community called to account at the end of time. The Judgement in the Marseille tradition follows the conventional Christian eschatological iconography.

major-21-le-monde.name: 21 — The World
major-21-le-monde.Scene: Le Monde (The World) in the Conver 1760 shows a nude female figure dancing or striding within a laurel wreath oval (mandorla), her body in the contrapposto posture of classical dance. She holds two wands (one in each hand) and her lower body is draped with a red sash. The mandorla is surrounded by the four fixed signs of the zodiac at the corners: the lion (Leo, fire), the eagle (Scorpio, water), the man or angel (Aquarius, air), and the bull (Taurus, earth). The World dancer moves within the completed cosmos, the whole of creation summarized in her dance.

coins-ace.name: Ace of Coins
coins-ace.Scene: The Ace of Coins (As de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille shows a single large coin or disc within a decorative floral or foliage surround — the centered pip as the concentrated emblem of the suit. The woodblock printing renders the coin face and its ornamental frame in the bold line style of the Marseille tradition, the suit symbol isolated as the seed of all material potential.

coins-02.name: Two of Coins
coins-02.Scene: The Two of Coins (Deux de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows two large coin pips connected by a figure-eight or S-shaped ribbon or band — the characteristic Marseille two of coins with its connecting band that links the two discs. This distinctive element (absent in many later decks) makes the two of coins a symbol of the material dynamic: two things in connection, balanced and exchanging.

coins-03.name: Three of Coins
coins-03.Scene: The Three of Coins (Trois de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows three coin pips arranged in a triangular pattern — two at the top and one below, or one above and two below — within a floral or geometric decorative frame. The Marseille three-of-coins follows the playing card convention of geometric pip arrangement.

coins-04.name: Four of Coins
coins-04.Scene: The Four of Coins (Quatre de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows four coin pips in a square arrangement within a decorative frame. The four coins are arranged at the four corners of the card's center field, their geometric regularity reflecting the stable, foundational quality of the number four in the material suit.

coins-05.name: Five of Coins
coins-05.Scene: The Five of Coins (Cinq de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows five coin pips in an X or quincunx arrangement — four at the corners and one at the center. In the Marseille tradition, the five of coins is the suit's mid-point disruption, the odd number that tips the balance of the stable four.

coins-06.name: Six of Coins
coins-06.Scene: The Six of Coins (Six de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows six coin pips in two rows of three or three rows of two, the even arrangement of the suit at six. The geometric regularity of the Marseille six-of-coins pip arrangement reflects the balanced distribution of material resources.

coins-07.name: Seven of Coins
coins-07.Scene: The Seven of Coins (Sept de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows seven coin pips in a pattern that typically has three in a row and then offsets — the odd number that exceeds the balanced six without reaching the even eight. In the Marseille tradition, the seven of coins is associated with the patient threshold of material waiting.

coins-08.name: Eight of Coins
coins-08.Scene: The Eight of Coins (Huit de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows eight coin pips in four rows of two or two rows of four — the even multiplication of the suit at eight. In the Marseille tradition, the eight of coins represents the methodical accumulation of material skill and resources.

coins-09.name: Nine of Coins
coins-09.Scene: The Nine of Coins (Neuf de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows nine coin pips in three rows of three — the three-by-three square of material near-completion. The nine of coins in the Marseille tradition represents refined material comfort and self-sufficiency.

coins-10.name: Ten of Coins
coins-10.Scene: The Ten of Coins (Dix de Deniers) in the Conver 1760 shows ten coin pips in rows or a pyramid arrangement — the complete expression of the material suit. In the Marseille tradition, the ten of coins is the apex of material accumulation and generational wealth.

coins-page.name: Page of Coins
coins-page.Scene: The Valet de Deniers (Page/Valet of Coins) in the Conver 1760 shows a young male figure in profile or three-quarters, holding the coin emblem in his hand and looking at it attentively. He wears the parti-colored clothing of a court page in the Marseille tradition — the bold woodblock colors of blue, red, and yellow — with a feathered hat. The Valet is the youngest male court figure, a diligent student of material matters who studies the coin with the focused attention of the practical learner.

coins-knight.name: Knight of Coins
coins-knight.Scene: The Cavalier de Deniers (Knight of Coins) in the Conver 1760 shows a mounted male figure in armor, holding the coin emblem and riding a horse that moves at a walk or gentle pace. The horse in the coins court cards typically moves more slowly than those in the swords or batons suits — the Cavalier de Deniers is the most methodical and patient of the mounted court figures. He wears the armor and hat of the Marseille court tradition.

coins-queen.name: Queen of Coins
coins-queen.Scene: The Reine de Deniers (Queen of Coins) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned female figure seated on a throne, holding the coin emblem and turning slightly to face the viewer. Her elaborate court dress in the Marseille primary colors — red, blue, yellow — and her crown reflect the high feminine authority of the material suit. The Queen of Coins is a figure of practical generosity and material stewardship.

coins-king.name: King of Coins
coins-king.Scene: The Roi de Deniers (King of Coins) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned male figure enthroned or seated, holding the coin emblem in one hand and a scepter in the other. His armor and crown in the Marseille primary colors reflect the highest male authority of the material suit. The King of Coins is the master of earthly resources and practical competence.

cups-ace.name: Ace of Cups
cups-ace.Scene: The Ace of Cups (As de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows a large ornate chalice or cup within a decorative frame, often with a host, dove, or rays emanating from it. The Marseille Ace of Cups is typically an elaborate architectural vessel — a large chalice with a wide base and ornamental cup — placed centrally in the card's field, the concentrated emblem of the emotional and spiritual suit.

cups-02.name: Two of Cups
cups-02.Scene: The Two of Cups (Deux de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows two cup pips arranged in bilateral symmetry — the suit's first division into the dyad of emotional exchange and mutual offering.

cups-03.name: Three of Cups
cups-03.Scene: The Three of Cups (Trois de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows three cup pips in a triangular arrangement — the communal triad of the emotional suit.

cups-04.name: Four of Cups
cups-04.Scene: The Four of Cups (Quatre de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows four cup pips in a square arrangement — the stable quadrant of the emotional suit.

cups-05.name: Five of Cups
cups-05.Scene: The Five of Cups (Cinq de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows five cup pips in a quincunx or asymmetric arrangement — the mid-point disruption of the emotional suit.

cups-06.name: Six of Cups
cups-06.Scene: The Six of Cups (Six de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows six cup pips in even rows — the balanced emotional abundance of the suit at six.

cups-07.name: Seven of Cups
cups-07.Scene: The Seven of Cups (Sept de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows seven cup pips in an asymmetric arrangement — the emotional suit at its threshold of excess, the proliferation of vessels before the even eight.

cups-08.name: Eight of Cups
cups-08.Scene: The Eight of Cups (Huit de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows eight cup pips in four pairs or rows — the even doubling of the emotional suit at eight.

cups-09.name: Nine of Cups
cups-09.Scene: The Nine of Cups (Neuf de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows nine cup pips in the three-by-three arrangement — the emotional near-completion, abundance one step before the full ten.

cups-10.name: Ten of Cups
cups-10.Scene: The Ten of Cups (Dix de Coupes) in the Conver 1760 shows ten cup pips in the final arrangement of the suit — the complete emotional abundance of the cups at its apex.

cups-page.name: Page of Cups
cups-page.Scene: The Valet de Coupes (Page of Cups) in the Conver 1760 shows a young male figure holding a cup and often glancing at it or looking beyond it. He wears the parti-colored court clothing of the Marseille tradition, a young person of emotional curiosity and imaginative sensitivity who carries the cup suit's emblem with attentive receptivity.

cups-knight.name: Knight of Cups
cups-knight.Scene: The Cavalier de Coupes (Knight of Cups) in the Conver 1760 shows a mounted male figure carrying a cup, his horse in a gentle or forward-stepping posture. The Cavalier de Coupes is the romantic messenger of the suit, riding forward with the cup held out as an offering or invitation. His armor and hat are in the Marseille court colors.

cups-queen.name: Queen of Cups
cups-queen.Scene: The Reine de Coupes (Queen of Cups) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned female figure seated on a throne, holding a covered or ornate cup and gazing forward or slightly aside. Her elaborate court dress in the Marseille primary colors reflects the high feminine authority of the emotional suit — deep feeling, intuition, and compassionate understanding embodied in the queen's seated authority.

cups-king.name: King of Cups
cups-king.Scene: The Roi de Coupes (King of Cups) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned male figure enthroned, holding an ornate cup scepter and sitting with the relaxed authority of emotional maturity. His crown and regalia in the Marseille primary colors reflect the apex of masculine authority in the emotional suit — wisdom in feeling, the balance of intellect and heart.

swords-ace.name: Ace of Swords
swords-ace.Scene: The Ace of Swords (As d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows a single upright sword within a crown or palm-and-olive-branch decoration — a large blade held vertically with decorative foliage and a crown at the top. The concentrated emblem of the mental and martial suit, the Ace of Swords in the Marseille tradition is an imposing solitary blade.

swords-02.name: Two of Swords
swords-02.Scene: The Two of Swords (Deux d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows two sword pips crossed or arranged in bilateral symmetry — the tension of two blades in opposition or negotiation.

swords-03.name: Three of Swords
swords-03.Scene: The Three of Swords (Trois d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows three sword pips in a triangular or vertical arrangement — the suit at three, the triangular tension of the blade suit.

swords-04.name: Four of Swords
swords-04.Scene: The Four of Swords (Quatre d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows four sword pips in a cross or square arrangement — the stable quadrant of the mental suit.

swords-05.name: Five of Swords
swords-05.Scene: The Five of Swords (Cinq d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows five sword pips in an asymmetric arrangement — the mid-point disruption of the blade suit, sharp forces past the stable four.

swords-06.name: Six of Swords
swords-06.Scene: The Six of Swords (Six d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows six sword pips in even rows — the balanced arrangement of the blade suit at six.

swords-07.name: Seven of Swords
swords-07.Scene: The Seven of Swords (Sept d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows seven sword pips in an asymmetric arrangement — the suit at seven, the threshold before the even eight.

swords-08.name: Eight of Swords
swords-08.Scene: The Eight of Swords (Huit d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows eight sword pips in even rows or pairs — the even doubling of the blade suit at eight.

swords-09.name: Nine of Swords
swords-09.Scene: The Nine of Swords (Neuf d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows nine sword pips in the three-by-three arrangement — the mental near-completion, the suit at its most concentrated before the final ten.

swords-10.name: Ten of Swords
swords-10.Scene: The Ten of Swords (Dix d'Épées) in the Conver 1760 shows ten sword pips in the final arrangement of the suit — the complete expression of the blade suit at its apex.

swords-page.name: Page of Swords
swords-page.Scene: The Valet d'Épées (Page of Swords) in the Conver 1760 shows a young male figure in profile, holding an upright sword with both hands or in one hand while looking back or forward. He wears the parti-colored court clothing of the Marseille tradition, his posture alert and watchful — the vigilant young person who keeps a careful eye on the world around him.

swords-knight.name: Knight of Swords
swords-knight.Scene: The Cavalier d'Épées (Knight of Swords) in the Conver 1760 shows a mounted male figure with sword raised or extended, his horse in a galloping or rearing posture — the most dynamic of the mounted court figures, charging forward with the blade of decisive action. He wears the armor and hat of the Marseille court tradition.

swords-queen.name: Queen of Swords
swords-queen.Scene: The Reine d'Épées (Queen of Swords) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned female figure enthroned, holding an upright sword and often raising one hand in a gesture of acknowledgment or command. Her court dress in the Marseille primary colors reflects the high feminine authority of the mental suit — clarity, independence, and perception forged through experience.

swords-king.name: King of Swords
swords-king.Scene: The Roi d'Épées (King of Swords) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned male figure enthroned, holding an upright sword with authority and looking forward with a direct gaze. His crown and armor in the Marseille primary colors reflect the apex of masculine authority in the mental suit — intellectual command, the power of judgment and clear communication.

batons-ace.name: Ace of Batons
batons-ace.Scene: The Ace of Batons (As de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows a single knotted club or staff — the characteristic Marseille baton, a rough-hewn wooden club with budding knots or sprouts along its length, suggesting the living wood from which it was cut. The Ace of Batons in the Conver is held vertically within a decorative surround, the concentrated emblem of the fiery and creative suit.

batons-02.name: Two of Batons
batons-02.Scene: The Two of Batons (Deux de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows two knotted club pips crossed or arranged in bilateral symmetry — the first division of the suit's creative potential.

batons-03.name: Three of Batons
batons-03.Scene: The Three of Batons (Trois de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows three knotted club pips in a triangular or vertical arrangement — the suit at three, the triangular expansion of creative fire.

batons-04.name: Four of Batons
batons-04.Scene: The Four of Batons (Quatre de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows four knotted club pips in a cross or square arrangement — the stable foundation of the creative suit.

batons-05.name: Five of Batons
batons-05.Scene: The Five of Batons (Cinq de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows five knotted club pips in an asymmetric arrangement — the mid-point disruption of the creative suit.

batons-06.name: Six of Batons
batons-06.Scene: The Six of Batons (Six de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows six knotted club pips in even rows — the balanced creative abundance of the suit at six.

batons-07.name: Seven of Batons
batons-07.Scene: The Seven of Batons (Sept de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows seven knotted club pips in an asymmetric arrangement — the creative suit at its threshold, courage and persistence before the even eight.

batons-08.name: Eight of Batons
batons-08.Scene: The Eight of Batons (Huit de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows eight knotted club pips in even pairs or rows — the swift doubling of the creative suit, velocity of motion and communication.

batons-09.name: Nine of Batons
batons-09.Scene: The Nine of Batons (Neuf de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows nine knotted club pips in the three-by-three arrangement — the near-completion of the creative suit.

batons-10.name: Ten of Batons
batons-10.Scene: The Ten of Batons (Dix de Bâtons) in the Conver 1760 shows ten knotted club pips in the final arrangement of the suit — the complete expression of creative energy at its apex.

batons-page.name: Page of Batons
batons-page.Scene: The Valet de Bâtons (Page of Batons) in the Conver 1760 shows a young male figure holding a knotted club upright, his posture alert and forward-facing. He wears the parti-colored court clothing of the Marseille tradition, a young person of creative enthusiasm and eager enterprise who carries the baton suit's emblem with confident, upright clarity.

batons-knight.name: Knight of Batons
batons-knight.Scene: The Cavalier de Bâtons (Knight of Batons) in the Conver 1760 shows a mounted male figure with a knotted club raised or held forward, his horse in a prancing or rearing posture — the dynamic creative rider who carries the suit's fire into active pursuit. He wears the hat and costume of the Marseille court tradition.

batons-queen.name: Queen of Batons
batons-queen.Scene: The Reine de Bâtons (Queen of Batons) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned female figure enthroned, holding a knotted club upright and facing forward with confident warmth. Her court dress in the Marseille primary colors reflects the high feminine authority of the creative suit — enthusiasm, generosity, and warm creative power.

batons-king.name: King of Batons
batons-king.Scene: The Roi de Bâtons (King of Batons) in the Conver 1760 shows a crowned male figure enthroned, holding a knotted club as his scepter of creative authority and looking forward with the confidence of a visionary leader. His crown and court dress in the Marseille primary colors reflect the apex of masculine authority in the creative suit — visionary enterprise and passionate leadership.

emg-majors.name: The 22 Trumps — The Marseille Standard
emg-majors.Scene: The 22 Major Arcana (Atouts or Trumps) of the Nicolas Conver Tarot de Marseille 1760 form the canonical Marseille trump sequence: the Fool (unnumbered), the Bateleur (I) through the World (XXI). This sequence represents the most definitive surviving reference point for the 'classical' Tarot de Marseille iconographic programme — Nicolas Conver's 1760 woodblock printing is the standard to which all scholarly discussions of the Marseille tradition refer. The Conver Majors reflect centuries of accumulated tradition in the French cardmaking center of Marseille.

emg-suit-coins.name: Suit of Coins (Deniers) — Earth
emg-suit-coins.Scene: The coins suit of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille comprises the Ace through Ten pip cards and four court ranks (Valet, Cavalier, Reine, Roi), totaling 14 cards. In the Conver woodblock printing, the coin pips are rendered as round disc emblems in bold Marseille coloring, and the courts are standing or mounted figures in parti-colored court dress. The coins suit of the Marseille tradition uses the geometric pip arrangement inherited from Italian playing cards.

emg-suit-cups.name: Suit of Cups (Coupes) — Water
emg-suit-cups.Scene: The cups suit of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille comprises the Ace through Ten pip cards and four court ranks, totaling 14 cards. The cup pips are rendered as ornate chalices in the Marseille woodblock style, and the courts show the four ranks in parti-colored court dress. The Ace of Cups in the Conver is a particularly elaborate architectural vessel.

emg-suit-swords.name: Suit of Swords (Épées) — Air
emg-suit-swords.Scene: The swords suit of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille comprises the Ace through Ten pip cards and four court ranks, totaling 14 cards. The sword pips are rendered as straight blades in the Marseille woodblock style, and the courts show the four ranks in parti-colored armored or court dress. The Cavalier de Bâtons (Knight of Swords) is typically the most dynamic of the mounted court figures.

emg-suit-batons.name: Suit of Batons (Bâtons) — Fire
emg-suit-batons.Scene: The batons suit of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille comprises the Ace through Ten pip cards and four court ranks, totaling 14 cards. The baton pips are rendered as knotted clubs with characteristic sprouts or knots suggesting living wood — a distinctive Marseille element — and the courts show the four ranks in parti-colored court dress. The knotted organic quality of the Marseille baton distinguishes it from the smooth wands of later occult decks.

kw-minor-arcana.name: Minor arcana
kw-minor-arcana.Scene: A keyword grouping for all 56 Minor Arcana cards of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the four suits of 14 cards each (Ace through Ten pips plus four courts). The Minor Arcana of the Marseille tradition use the pip-card style: suit symbols arranged in geometric patterns rather than the scenic illustrations that later characterize the Rider-Waite-Smith tradition. This geometric pip tradition reflects the Italian and French playing card heritage of the tarot's minor suits.

kw-major-arcana.name: Major arcana
kw-major-arcana.Scene: A keyword grouping for all 22 Major Arcana cards of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the trump sequence from the Fool (0) through the World (XXI). The Conver Major Arcana are the definitive reference point for the classical Marseille iconographic programme, the most-cited and most-studied set of trump images in the scholarly and practitioner literature on the historical tarot.

kw-marseille.name: Marseille
kw-marseille.Scene: A keyword grouping identifying all items belonging to the Tarot de Marseille tradition as exemplified by Nicolas Conver's 1760 woodblock deck. 'Marseille' as a label covers the family of related French tarot decks produced in the French playing card center of Marseille from the 17th century onward, of which the Conver 1760 is the canonical reference edition. The Marseille tradition is characterized by its pip-card style, its specific trump iconography, and its four-rank courts (Valet, Cavalier, Reine, Roi).

kw-court-card.name: Court card
kw-court-card.Scene: A keyword grouping for all 16 court cards across the four suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille. The Marseille courts use a four-rank system: Valet (Page), Cavalier (Knight), Reine (Queen), and Roi (King). The Conver court cards are rendered in the bold woodblock primary colors of the Marseille tradition, the figures in parti-colored court dress against simple backgrounds.

kw-air.name: Air
kw-air.Scene: A keyword grouping for items associated with the element of Air in the Conver Tarot de Marseille — the mental, communicative, and sharp dimension of the suits. Air is traditionally associated with the swords suit: thought, conflict, speech, and the cutting clarity of the blade.

kw-batons.name: Batons
kw-batons.Scene: A keyword grouping for the batons suit — the knotted clubs that represent the creative, fiery, and enterprising suit of the Tarot de Marseille. The Marseille batons are distinctive for their organic, knotted quality: living wood rather than smooth wands, the rough material of creative enterprise.

kw-coins.name: Coins
kw-coins.Scene: A keyword grouping for the coins suit — the round discs that represent the material, earthly, and financial suit of the Tarot de Marseille. In the Conver 1760, the coins are depicted as bold circular emblems arranged in geometric pip patterns, the suit of earthly resources and practical concerns.

kw-cups.name: Cups
kw-cups.Scene: A keyword grouping for the cups suit — the ornate chalices that represent the emotional and spiritual suit of the Tarot de Marseille. In the Conver 1760, the cups are elaborately rendered vessels, the Ace of Cups being the most architecturally complex pip in the deck.

kw-earth.name: Earth
kw-earth.Scene: A keyword grouping for items associated with the element of Earth in the Conver Tarot de Marseille — the material, stable, and productive dimension of the suits. Earth is traditionally associated with the coins suit: physical resources, material accumulation, and the patient work of earthly life.

kw-fire.name: Fire
kw-fire.Scene: A keyword grouping for items associated with the element of Fire in the Conver Tarot de Marseille — the creative, passionate, and enterprising dimension of the suits. Fire is traditionally associated with the batons suit: energy, enthusiasm, and the spark of creative initiative.

kw-swords.name: Swords
kw-swords.Scene: A keyword grouping for the swords suit — the blades that represent the mental and martial suit of the Tarot de Marseille. In the Conver 1760, the swords are rendered as straight blades in geometric pip arrangements, the suit of thought, conflict, and the cutting precision of truthful discernment.

kw-water.name: Water
kw-water.Scene: A keyword grouping for items associated with the element of Water in the Conver Tarot de Marseille — the emotional, intuitive, and fluid dimension of the suits. Water is traditionally associated with the cups suit: feeling, imagination, and the receptive depth of the inner life.

kw-b-tons.name: Bâtons
kw-b-tons.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping for the batons suit using the French spelling 'Bâtons' (with circumflex) — the French cardmaking term for the clubs or staves suit as used in the Tarot de Marseille tradition.

kw-coupes.name: Coupes
kw-coupes.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping using the French name 'Coupes' for the cups suit — the French cardmaking term for the cups or chalices as used in the Tarot de Marseille tradition.

kw-deniers.name: Deniers
kw-deniers.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping using the French name 'Deniers' for the coins suit — the French cardmaking term for the coins or deniers (pennies) as used in the Tarot de Marseille tradition. Deniers is the French equivalent of the Italian 'Denari', both derived from the Roman denarius.

kw-p-es.name: Épées
kw-p-es.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping using the French name 'Épées' (with accent) for the swords suit — the French cardmaking term for the swords or épées as used in the Tarot de Marseille tradition.

kw-ace.name: Ace
kw-ace.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four aces across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille. The aces are the concentrated seeds of each suit — a single coin, a single cup, a single sword, a single knotted club — the undivided potential from which each suit's numerical expansion grows.

kw-cavalier.name: Cavalier
kw-cavalier.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four Cavalier (Knight) court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille. The Cavaliers are mounted male figures bearing each suit's emblem, the active and dynamic second rank of the Marseille court system. Each Cavalier's horse posture reflects the temperament of its suit: the Swords Cavalier charges, the Coins Cavalier walks methodically.

kw-eight.name: Eight
kw-eight.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four eight-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the geometric arrangement of eight pip symbols in the Marseille tradition.

kw-five.name: Five
kw-five.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four five-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the quincunx or asymmetric mid-point of each suit.

kw-four.name: Four
kw-four.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four four-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the stable quadrant arrangement of each suit.

kw-king.name: King
kw-king.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four Roi (King) court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the apex male court figures of each suit's hierarchy.

kw-knight.name: Knight
kw-knight.Scene: A keyword grouping for all Knight court figures — equivalent to the Cavaliers — across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille. In French tarot nomenclature, 'Cavalier' is the standard term, while 'Knight' is the English equivalent used in cross-tradition contexts.

kw-nine.name: Nine
kw-nine.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four nine-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the near-completion of each suit in the three-by-three arrangement.

kw-page.name: Page
kw-page.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four Valet (Page) court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille. In French tarot nomenclature, 'Valet' is the standard term for the lowest male court rank, while 'Page' is the English equivalent. The Valets are the youngest and most eager court figures, each bearing their suit's emblem with the attentiveness of a student.

kw-queen.name: Queen
kw-queen.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four Reine (Queen) court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the enthroned female figures who represent the high feminine authority of each suit.

kw-reine.name: Reine
kw-reine.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping using the French term 'Reine' for the Queen court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the French cardmaking term for the queen as used in the Tarot de Marseille tradition.

kw-roi.name: Roi
kw-roi.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping using the French term 'Roi' for the King court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the French cardmaking term for the king as used in the Marseille tradition.

kw-seven.name: Seven
kw-seven.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four seven-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the asymmetric arrangement of each suit at the patient threshold before eight.

kw-six.name: Six
kw-six.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four six-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the balanced even-row arrangement of each suit at six.

kw-ten.name: Ten
kw-ten.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four ten-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the completed expression of each suit in its final pip arrangement.

kw-three.name: Three
kw-three.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four three-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the triangular arrangement of each suit at three.

kw-two.name: Two
kw-two.Scene: A keyword grouping for all four two-pip cards across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the bilateral first division of each suit's undivided potential.

kw-valet.name: Valet
kw-valet.Scene: An alternate keyword grouping using the French term 'Valet' for the Page court figures across the suits of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille — the French cardmaking term for the youngest male court rank as used in the Tarot de Marseille tradition.

axis-keyword.name: By Keyword
axis-keyword.Scene: The keyword axis of the Nicolas Conver 1760 Tarot de Marseille organizes the deck's 118 items by thematic grouping — suits (French and English names), elements, pip numbers, court ranks (French and English), and the major/minor arcana distinction. This axis allows navigation across the canonical Marseille deck through the conceptual patterns that structure its 78 cards: the elemental suit system, the numerical pip progression, and the four-rank court hierarchy.
